Last Friday evening, April 16, I made reference to private bills which had been introduced in another place, where their standing committees were set up last December and some bills passed, whereas our committee was not set up until the end of February. For that reason I am told some lawyers thought it well to go to the other place to introduce these measures, and that this was the reason such action was being taken.
I did not wish to reflect upon those in another place, where there are able men of whom many formerly sat with me as colleagues, and all of whom have rendered real service. I have made it a rule to respect the views of others and to have pleasant relationships with all hon. members. Last Friday I said I had no intention of reflecting upon any hon. member here who might, have introduced a measure for some legal friend. I have not changed my views as to the usefulness of that other place in times so grave as these, and only desired a better study of all such bills.

For some time past the tonnage of steel plates available to the railway car builders has controlled their rate of operation. Generally speaking they are able to obtain sufficient other steel components to level off the tonnages of plates which have been made available.

Through 1947 the three car builders as a group received an average allocation of 3,000 tons of plates per month. During the first quarter of 1948 this total allocation was increased to 4,000 tons per month, but it was found impossible to continue at this rate, and the total allocation was reduced to 3,250 tons of plate per month for the second quarter, representing approximately eighty per cent of the first quarter allocation.
In order to reallocate the total tonnage of plates available for car building it has been necessary to have the transportation equipment committee, Department of Reconstruction and Supply, call a meeting of representatives from the three car building companies, who have arrived at the most equitable reallocation of available tonnage, having regard to labour in the respective plants.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the house rose yesterday afternoon I was dealing with some of the, ways in which the 21 per cent increase in freight rates will affect Saskatchewan and western Canada.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: May I call the attention of hon. gentlemen to the fact that there is so much talk going on that it is impossible to hear the hon. member who has the floor.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
I should like to refer again to what has already been placed on the record with respect to the way in which the 21 per cent increase in freight rates will affect the cost of shipping cattle to eastern Canada. The 21 per cent increase in the freight rates will reduce the price of a carload of cattle to the farmer by $50.05 when shipped from Crane Valley to Toronto.
Yesterday I referred to the fact that various decisions of the board of transport commissioners in the past have lessened the inequalities in the freight rates as between western and central Canada, but this latest increase has further widened inequalities that already existed.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I must ask hon. members to leave the chamber if they want to carry on conversation. I cannot hear what the hon. member is saying, and I think it is most unfair for those who want to talk to do so while he is speaking.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
For example, the cost of shipping 100 pounds of gasoline from Sarnia, Ontario, to a point 50 miles away is eight cents, whereas the freight charges for shipping 100 pounds of gasoline from Regina to a point 50 miles away is 20 cents, the difference between the two rates being 12 cents. The 21 per cent increase in the freight rates will increase the cost of the shipment of gasoline from Sarnia by 1-6 cents but it will increase the cost of the shipment from Regina by 4-2 cents. Instead of having the previous spread of 12 cents between these two shipments, the new rates increase the spread to 14-6 cents. It can thus be seen that the 21 per cent increase in freight rates is further aggravating the inequalities that existed in the past.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) placed a table on the record to show that increased freight charges on certain articles shipped from western Canada to central Canada were not very great. His figures showed that the increased freight rates on a dozen eggs when shipped in a carload lot amounted to just one-tenth of a cent. While that may be true, the fact remains that the minimum charges have been increased by more than 21 per cent. The minimum charge for a
Freight Rates

shipment of less than 100 pounds has been increased from 50 to 75 cents.
Everyone knows that farmers in western Canada who ship eggs and cream ship them in lots of less than 100 pounds. It now means that there is an increase of 25 cents in the cost of each shipment. This means an increase of 25 cents, or approximately two cents per dozen, in the cost of shipping a 12 dozen crate of eggs. Similarly on a shipment of a crate of 30 dozen eggs the freight cost will be increased by five-sixths of a cent per dozen. So the effect of the freight rate increase will be much more than one-tenth of a cent per dozen, as outlined by the transport minister, and will in fact amount to an increase in freight charges on eggs of from one cent to more than two cents per dozen.
The same thing applies with respect to the shipment of cream. Farmers usually ship cream to the creamery in three-gallon or five-gallon cans. A five-gallon can of cream, testing 35 per cent butter fat, produces approximately 17| pounds of butter fat, and the increased cost of 25 cents on that can of cream will amount to approximately 1! cents on a pound of butter fat. The increased cost on a shipment of a three-gallon can of cream will amount to approximately 2! cents per pound of butter fat. It is not correct, therefore, to say that the only increase in freight costs as they affect butter will amount to one-tenth of a cent when butter is shipped. It will amount to one-tenth of a cent, plus from 1! to 2| cents per pound of butter fat, when cream is shipped to the creamery.
The railways when putting their case before the board of transport commissioners pleaded that they were in great financial need and that it was necessary that an increase be granted immediately. But counsel for Saskatchewan pointed out that the Canadian Pacific Railway was not in financial difficulties, that in its 1946 balance sheet was an item of $77,870,000 which had been accumulated from earnings, and the justification for that accumulation must have been that a situation might arise calling for the use of additional funds during an emergency. Placing its case before the board of transport commissioners in 1946, the C.P.R. estimated that its 1947 net railway earnings would be $14,800,000. But when the balance sheet for 1947 was made public it showed net railway earnings of $22,892,189. Thus the C.P.R. in fact in 1947 made $8,000,000 more than it had estimated when placing its case before the board. It cannot be said therefore that the C.P.R. today is in great financial need and that it needs a 21 per cent increase in freight rates.

The chief commissioner's report sets out the various items for which the Canadian Pacific, according to the commissioner, requires revenue. He gives a figure of $15,235,000 for surplus, $21,000,000 for dividends, and more than $15,000,000 for fixed charges. The chief commissioner said in his judgment:	We will
give to the C.P.R. sufficient revenue to cover its fixed charges and to pay four per cent on the preferred stock and five per cent on the common stock. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that five per cent is a high rate in view of prevailing interest rates today. The commissioner went on to say:	Not only will we guarantee the
C.P.R. a high rate of return upon its investments but in addition we will allow it a surplus of $15,235,000. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the board of transport commissioners and the government should not have permitted an increase that takes hard-earned money from the common people of Canada in order that the C.P.R. may pay big dividends and have a surplus of more than $15,000,000 per year.
The financial position of the C.P.R. has improved tremendously over the past number of years. At the end of 1947 its funded debt had been reduced $7,700,000 as compared with 1946. Its reserves in 1947 had increased by approximately $30,000,000 over 1946. Its funded debt in 1937 was $228,000,000, and in 1947, $95,301,000. a reduction in ten years of $153,000,000. The reserves of the C.P.R. in 1937 were $91,000,000 and in 1947, $379,905,000, or an increase in ten years of almost $289,000,000.
I suggest that those figures, Mr. Speaker, prove beyond doubt that the C.P.R. is not in great financial need, and in fact does not need an increase in freight rates.
Over the past years the railways have always made a greater profit on their western than on their eastern lines. Between the years 1936 and 1946 the C.P.R. made a profit on its western lines of more than $248,000,000, while on its eastern lines it made a profit of $126,000,000. That proves, I submit, that the C.P.R., because of higher freight rates in western Canada, made large profits from its western operations as compared with its profits in eastern Canada, and such discrimination cannot be justified to this house.
Over the years governments in this country have taken a very benevolent interest in the C.P.R. If the board of transport commissioners are right, and the railways need this increase, I am satisfied that the people of the prairie provinces, who are eminently fair-minded,-if they felt that it was a question on the one hand of an increase in freight rates and on the other financial chaos for the railways, in spite of the fact that they do not like high freight rates the people would realize in their common sense and judgment that we must have increased freight rates and that they would have to share in the increase as do the other parts of Canada.

Those of us who come from
western Canada should be concerning ourselves with this. That is what affects us in the western prairie provinces, and that is why I am raising the point today.
I am not sure that the terms of reference protect the prairie provinces. Let me read from P.C. 1487, which is the order in council in question. It reads in part as follows:
It is therefore advisable that the board of transport commissioners for Canada be directed to make a thorough investigation of the rates structure of railways and railway companies which are under the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rates structure which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities in the various provinces and territories of Canada, so as to permit the freest possible handling of commodities.
What is new about that? The reference has to do with the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, do certain things. The application of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta re alteration in the terminal tariffs, involving elimination of the assumed mileage between Port Arthur and Winnipeg was dismissed upon the ground that the general advantage accruing from the latter feature in the rate structure did not warrant any change being made.
I do not know whether anything in our changed economy has changed that. I know the government does not like too well to accept suggestions from the opposition, but I wish to suggest this to them. The time has come, particularly in these serious days, when the opposition's suggestions should be seriously listened to and considered. There would not have been this discrimination if the government had carried out the suggestion urged upon them at that time by the hon. member for Calgary West in this House of Commons as long ago as March 6, 1947, namely that there be an inquiry into the discrimination with regard to rates and the formulation of an equalization plan.

Well, Mr. Speaker, here is one who disagrees with that suggestion. Last week the financial statement of the C.P.R. was published. On all operations of the company the profits amounted to $31,893,942 in 1947, an increase of $6,759,211 over the previous year. Stockholders received $2.04 per share as compared with the $1.53 they got in 1946, an increase of 33^ per cent. Of course it is argued that operating costs of all kinds have gone up and will go up; but if the traffic also goes up, if the business increases at the same rate as last year, even at the old charges another considerable increase in net profits would be indicated. If, however, the railways simply have to have more money, it would have been fairly simple to leave the prairie and maritime schedules as they were and raise the rates in eastern Canada to the levels being charged on the prairies. This situation will give another incentive to the western provinces especially to get into industry as speedily as possible and so avoid payment of much of the freight now being charged. We can build more crushing mills to take care of all the flaxseed grown in the west, more woollen mills and factories to manufacture our wool clip, more tanneries, more boot and shoe, factories, more pulp and paper mills and a host of other industries to take care of the products of the west. We have plenty of water power for the production of electricity; we have coal deposits galore, and

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the house for any great length of time in the discussion of this subject, although it is one of the most important which will come before the House of Commons this year. Certainly it is of great importance to both western and eastern Canada.
I am not taking exception to the findings of the board of transport commissioners in connection with the increase of 21 per cent in the rate. I believe the railroads, without difficulty, established the necessity for some additional revenue. I believe additional revenue was necessary, not only to be able to pay dividends to the stockholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway, but so that that company, as well as the nationally owned system, might be placed1 in a position where they could stand on their own feet, and even make returns sufficient to instil confidence in Ihe minds of the investing public. This would be necessary if later they found it necessary to sell bonds for the improvement of rolling stock. It would be a sad day for Canada if the C.P.R. ever reached the position -where the government and the Canadian people had to take it over, to be operated in conjunction with the Canadian National Railways.
Unless they are allowed to earn sufficient money to induce additional capital they cannot keep their rolling stock in a condition which would be competitive with that of United States railways. In my opinion that would be a bad position indeed. The worst factor of all is that they would not be able to perform the services which they should perform, namely, the giving to the Canadian people of as good freight and passenger service as is offered by any other transportation company in or outside of Canada.
I believe it is necessary to maintain this condition, and I believe that in giving relief the board of transport commissioners transferred the burden to the shoulders of the manufacturers and producers of the far east and the far west. Therefore it has now become necessary as soon as possible to address ourselves to the problem of finding an equitable rate structure upon which we can operate.
Freight Rates

That is my principal reason for speaking today. I do not rise to justify what has been done; rather I am speaking in an appeal to the minister to see that the board of transport commissioners bring about an equalization of freight rates without delay. If this load must be carried by the Canadian people, it must be carried on an equitable basis, or there will be difficulty. Confederation became an actuality with the building of the railways; I fear that it will go out of existence if we do not have it on a proper basis. I do not believe we can build a second story on this freight rate structure unless we are prepared to go right down to the foundation, begin over again and do it right. I am prepared to give the board of transport commissioners adequate time to do that job, but I do not want to give them one minute more than is necessary.
As I said before, to get the money to keep the railway rolling stock in good condition it was necessary to treat the railways and railway employees well. But what is happening now? The far eastern manufacturers and producers, as well as those in the far west, find that they have this 21 per cent increase piled on top of a rate which already is high. They are driven to the point where they must do business from 350 to 400 miles closer to their own doorstep. In other words there are many manufacturers in the west who have been enjoying business in the mid western provinces who will not now be able to carry on with that business for any great length of time. Certainly from their point of view there is urgency to have this matter settled as quickly as possible.
I have spoken about manufacturers. I now turn to one of our major industries on the Pacific coast, that of shipbuilding. Steel for their ships will cost the yards another 21 per cent. Those yards will be put out of line with yards in eastern Canada, and particularly those in the central provinces. It is necessary that that industry be protected particularly in respect of the shipment of steel into British Columbia. It may be that we are now in a somewhat better position, because it is possible that with more ships available we shall be able to bring steel in by water. But will that help the railways in their province? They will lose that volume of trade as well as the revenue derived therefrom. 8o for their own good I think it is necessary that that business be retained.
We do not like to feel that we are being crowded back onto our own doorsteps so far as the development of our industry is concerned. The other day the hon. member for 
Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters) said that we want to be independent, that we want to stand on our own feet. That is true, but we want a place to stand. And the way things are going at the present time we are not being given a place to stand.
We have no outlook for our business, either in the west or in the east unless some adjustments are made. This is true not only of shipbuilding but also of the poultry and egg business. Certainly it is true of the tree fruits industry. I understand that the extra cost to that industry this year will be about a million dollars, and one cannot say what it will be for the lumber industry.
There are two points in connection with freight rates which I do not think require any further argument, adjustment, or meetings of the board. The first of these is the mountain differential. This matter has been argued year after year before board after board, and it has been agreed that the mountain rate should be taken off in nearly every instance. I believe that, without going too far at all, that is one place where the minister could act now, by asking the board to give a ruling without delay-right away. This would give considerable relief.

Is there any justice in that kind of set-up? I cannot see it at all. The same commodity travels over the same railroad, but in one case it goes east and in the other it goes west. Surely these two things do not require any further consideration.
Personally I cannot see why the people of Ontario and Quebec are not more interested in this matter. Surely they realize what is bound to happen. When you have railroad rates piled too high they become a tariff which makes industry in one locality permanently secure. Who wants such security? At the same time industry in Ontario and Quebec is kept out of certain areas. What will happen?
Iam going to tell you that if I were a few years younger and thinking of going into business I would look very carefully at Winnipeg's position, and I certainly would look with longing eyes at the position of Edmonton as a manufacturing centre under the high rate structure we have at the present time. The people of Ontario and Quebec cannot sit idly by and see inequality piled up as between the east and the west. Eventually it will prove to their disadvantage.
It may be thought from what I have said that I should support one of the amendments. I am not going to support the C.C.F. amendment because it means a vote of want of confidence. Who has ever heard of a government being thrown out of office because it supported the action of its own creature? That is what the board of transport commissioners is. It would be something new so far as I am concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house is becoming impatient and is anxious to vote on the amendment proposed by the leader of this group, but as I spoke last year on the subject of freight rates when the 30 per cent application was presented to the board of transport commissioners I feel that I would be remiss in my duty if I did not protest on this occasion about the increase recently granted.
I wish to add my voice in further protest against the additional burden which has been placed upon the prairies and the maritime provinces which already provide more than their fair share of the operating revenues of the Canadian railway systems. The argument advanced in favour of the 21 per cent increase in freight rates is the same as that which has been advanced by industry in favour of higher prices for consumer goods, namely, increased operating costs on account of higher prices required for materials and higher wages for employees.
I submit that the argument that more revenue is necessary in order to pay increased wages is an attempt on the part of the railroads to throw the onus on the employees of the railway systems for the recent 21 per cent increase in freight rates. This is unfair, because, during the war and subsequently when the railroads had the highest revenues in their history, they had ample opportunity to improve the lot of their employees. But what happened? The wages of the men barely kept pace with dhe increased cost of living.
Railway maintenance men, shop men and porters are still underpaid. They have never received wages commensurate with the onerous tasks they perform. The basis of the demand for this 21 per cent increase is not increased wages for employees; it is because greater revenue is required in the case of the Canadian National Raihvays to service an unwieldy debt, and in the case of the Canadian Pacific Company to meet the demands of the shareholders for more dividends. The government could have prevented this 21 per cent increase had price control been retained.

Railway employees have repeatedly told me-this is in answer to my hon. friend who interjected-that if the government had retained price control they would not now require increased wages. They feel this way about it, that if they do get a slight increase in wages, everything they purchase for themselves and their families will go up in price so much that their wages will fall far short of their needs. They know, and this house knows, that wages never keep pace with mounting living costs. The whole freight rate issue, as I see it, is just another chicken come home to roost. It is one of the fruits of the government's reckless and ill-conoeived decontrol policy. Had price control been retained, the price level of materials required by the railways, and the wage level necessary- to maintain the standards of living of their employees, could have remained such as to make it quite unnecessary for increased revenue demands by the railways at this time. Certainly the railways would have under those circumstances no argument to substantiate a demand for higher freight rates. The government therefore must take full responsibility for the situation which has led to the 21 per cent increase in freight rates.
To give the railways a blood transfusion of a 21 per cent increase in freight rates when they are in a relatively healthy position is in my opinion quite unjustifiable. I would ask what has happened to the reserves, which, according to "Railways in Canada, 1945", a publication issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce, had reached at the end of 1945 the sum of S493 million. What has become of these reserves?
The main opposition to the increase is, however, based upon the fact that it imposes an added burden upon a freight rate structure already discriminatory in effect upon the west and upon the maritimes. It places an intolerable burden on the economy of these regions. It is a severe blow to the economy of the prairies and of the provinces down by the sea. It intensifies the discrimination in freight rates as between the central provinces and the remainder of the dominion. There is not the least doubt that it will have a disruptive effect upon the Canadian economy as a whole. It contributes to inflation and will increase most substantially the cost of living of the people of the prairies and of the maritimes. According to a report in Time magazine of April 12, the new rates will take $70 million out of the pockets of Canadians, particularly in the maritimes and in western Canada. There has already been a noticeable increase in the mark-up of goods in various parts of Canada
	.
since this 21 per cent increase. For instance, in Vancouver, automobiles and trucks are now up from $25 to $50. In Halifax steak is up twelve cents a pound and tea up ten cents a pound.
According to an article appearing in the Regina Leader-Post of March 31, a paper that is most friendly to the government, the new rates will boost lumber costs $3 per 1,000 feet, canned goods forty cents a case, farm tractors from $8 to $14 apiece, coal twenty-five cents a ton and fertilizer forty cents a ton or more. In other words, the grocery bill and fuel, clothing and construction costs will be greatly increased. Furthermore, the heavier rates will increase the cost of production for the farmer, since gasoline, farm machinery and other commodities which go into his production costs will all cost more money. This will force the farmer in turn to demand a higher price for his produce in order to make ends meet.
Prairie people, and I am sure maritimers as well, are quite prepared to assume their fair share of transportation costs. I refer to the maritimes deliberately, Mr. Speaker, because I am a maritimer by birth and I have some real reason for bringing this part of the country into any speech on freight rates. I am sure that both the prairies and the maritimes are quite prepared to assume their fair share of transportation costs, but the rates in these regions, even prior to the recent increase of 21 per cent, were higher than in the central provinces. On the prairies, for instance, they were 15 per cent higher. A freight rate in Ontario of $1 becomes $1.15 on the western plains. This is the main reason for the opposition to the flat increase of 21 per cent across the board, recently permitted by the board of transport commissioners and sanctioned by the federal government.
The prairies have always provided top operating revenue for the railways. According to figures released in the equalization of rates case in 1927, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's net earnings in the western region were double those received in its eastern region. The freight rate structure has not been materially altered since that time until the present 21 per cent increase was granted. Therefore the same situation prevailed until 1948. Operations in eastern Canada have been less profitable for the railways because of greater competition, which has been referred to again and again in this house, and because of heavier maintenance charges to which the railways there have been subject. This has made a difference in the net revenue in the two regions. But in the case of the prairies it seems grossly unfair to discriminate against them in this matter just to provide additional

Freight Rates
revenue for the railways in order to meet the deficits which they may accumulate in the eastern region.
Last year when I spoke on this subject I said:
There should be no attempt to be unfair to the railways. On the other hand, if an over-all increase in freight rates is discriminatory in effect it may have dangerous consequences.
I still think so, Mr. Speaker. I continue with the quotation:
The imposition of an unfair and unwieldy freight structure upon any region of Canada can well develop an anti-confederation attitude. This has manifested itself on several occasions, both in the maritimes and in the west. This, of course, is to be avoided. All Canadians must remember that confederation should be based on equality and that economic discrimination against any area in the dominion may create separatist sentiments. I suggest that now is the opportune time to examine the whole freight rate structure so as to remove existing inequalities.
Remember, Mr. Speaker, that is what I said last year when the application was being submitted to the board for an increase in freight rates. I continue the quotation:
Now is the time to set up a royal commission, if you will, to investigate thoroughly all charges of discrimination which have been levelled against the railways by western and other organizations. I submit that, until this whole matter is ironed out to the satisfaction of both the^ west and the maritimes, no body is in any position to appraise the need for a general increase in railway rates of any kind.
But the increase has been allowed without any attempt being made to remove the discrimination in rates which exists. That was the mistake which was made. Now the minister states, in an afterthought, that the present board of transport commissioners will be instructed to conduct an inquiry into alleged discrimination in the rates schedule. This is not a hopeful augury. The board has now' been occupied for more than a year inquiring into the sufficiency of the present rates, and to appoint such a board to go into the whole rate structure will be in effect asking it simply to review its own findings. Surely this should have been done-

Speaker, I should like to say that the government has been aware of the discriminatory rates condition for some time, and certainly we have not been remiss in our duty in this corner of the house for we have brought it to the attention of the government on several occasions. Material in the hands of the board also substantiates the fact that such a condition prevails. I am quite certain that the seven provinces concerned in this matter will not be very well satisfied with this afterthought on the part of the minister. The people of the west and the maritimes want action, and they want that action now.
Furthermore, I think the public in the seven provinces concerned will demand that a wholly independent body, untrammeled by past rulings, precedents and judgments, be set up to deal with this urgent matter. The matter of freight rate discrimination should be dealt with in a wholly objective manner. This is a job for a royal commission, and I urge upon the minister to restore public confidence by setting up such a body. I do not feel that much will be gained by the reviewer reviewing its own findings or its own judgments. A royal commission completely independent should be appointed to examine the host of questions affecting public policy in this regard, and to bring in a report to parliament as expeditiously as possible.
I question the competency of the present board to deal with this subject, a board appointed to control railway rates and practices, and I say that, Mr. Speaker, despite what the minister said this afternoon to the effect that the board has power to deal with equalization of rates. If power exists, why has it not been used? This is a very important matter; it is a matter of freight rate differential, and it affects the economy of the country. Furthermore, the subject of freight rate discrimination appears completely outside the sphere of authority of the board on this matter, or it should have been dealt with long ago.
I believe., however, that any commission of inquiry which might be appointed should act and act quickly. There has been a public apathy toward certain of these commissions in the past. There is good reason for it, because they have too often been abortive of results, and public suspicion of them is to some extent well founded. The reports of many royal commissions are gathering dust in the archives of this nation and have been doing so for many years. I suggest, therefore, that a year on such an inquiry is ample time, for if a longer period were taken it would only promote a

lack of confidence and intensify the agitation which already exists in both the west and the maritimes against the decision of the board and against the railways as a whole. Such a commission should, in my opinion, be instructed to act with dispatch and to submit a report not later than the next session of parliament. Such a body could examine the effects of the whole freight rate structure upon our whole economic life.
In conclusion, I wish to say that I believe freight rates on essential goods should be held to a minimum. Moreover, there must not be regional discrimination. If periods should occur when operating expenses exceed revenues, the nation as a whole should be responsible for the deficits. All parts of Canada should assume a part of that burden if it should occur. The future welfare of Canada as a nation may well be at stake if rates are to vary in different parts of the country. Moreover, it is time that the dependence of the railways on the west for top operating revenue stopped. Until now the west has carried the major load in providing the railway system with profits. All the west and the maritimes are now asking is that they, as a part of this nation, be accorded a square deal in this urgent matter that affects their economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I fully appreciate that hon. members want to get through with this debate; but if they had received the letters and resolutions I have received they would feel as I do, that it is my duty to say a few words in support of this amendment. I have boiled down what I should like to have said into a short speech, and I hope I may have the privilege of delivering it now.
It would seem to me that the board of transport commissioners, in allowing a horizontal increase, has not carried out the intention of the Railway Act. Section 31 of that act deals with the matter of equity with respect to tolls and facilities. In effect the section says there shall be equality as to tolls with respect to all classes carried under substantially the same circumstances and conditions, and no toll shall be charged which unjustly discriminates between different localities. The two principal considerations governing the board are, 5849-2054
first, as to the reasonableness of the rate, and, second, whether or not there is the feature of unjust discrimination.
Many instances of discrimination and injustice have been cited by hon. members in all parts of the house and belonging to all parties in the house, and I do not intend to take time to go farther into those discriminations. I wish to point out, however, that we have had increases in freight rates in the past. The first increase, following the first world war, came in 1917, when they were increased 15 per cent. The second increase was in 1918, and was 25 per cent, while the third increase came in 1920. The increase in 1920, however, was not horizontal. That is the point I wish to make. The board in the past has made at least one increase where the increase was not horizontal and was different in different parts of Canada. For instance, in eastern Canada the increase was 40 per cent and, in western Canada, 35 per cent, and on the transcontinental rates it was 33J per cent, subject to certain exemptions.
My contention is that the board knows and has known that there has been discrimination for years. It seems to me that when the board allowed a horizontal increase it took the easy way out. Had the board increased freight rates in a manner similar to that which was done in 1920, allowing an increase of 30 per cent in eastern Canada and 10 per cent in western Canada, there would ffot have been such a protest made as has been made by the western and maritime provinces. This would, of course, have required more work and more study as to what actual percentages of increase should have been allowed.
Much has been said about the Canadian National Railways and their needs. My colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) made what I thought was an excellent analysis of the balance sheet of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I am not going to deal with the Canadian Pacific this afternoon. The figures which he gave at that time will have to be answered by the government and by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) before this debate is concluded.
In considering the need of the Canadian National Railways I think it is essential that this house take a look at the financial structure of that corporation, and I should like to quote from the judgment of the board of transport commissioners in this regard:
The'situation in respect to Canadian National Railways is quite different today to the situation prevailing in 1929 or even in 1925. The railways are now fully integrated into one great railway transportation system which is well and efficiently operated and managed. Furthermore, the Canadian National Railways Capital Revisions
Freight Rates

Act, 1937 (Canada, chapter 22, 1937), went a long way towards alleviating the financial burden carried by the railway. One of the results of the adjustments which were made by the said act, in the balance sheet of the Canadian National Railways in 1937, was to reduce by $35,900,600 the amount of interest payable by the Canadian National to the government of Canada, the proprietors, on moneys advanced by the parliament of Canada to the railways to defray operating deficits incurred prior to 1937.
In 1936 the fixed charges were shown for the Canadian National Railways at $86,995,878; in 1937 they had decreased to $51,597,321, and in 1946, through refinancing during the war, to $46,104,626.
In 1939 the interest on government loans amounted to $916,165, but in 1946 this item had reached the total of $21,322,583. Mr. Vaughan, president of Canadian National Railways, in his statement before the board, on the present application, repeated his suggestion which was previously made to the railways committee of the House of Commons "that at least this amount of $400,000,000 which the government had loaned- for the purpose of repatriating securities should be placed on an income bond basis," that is, that the interest on this amount would be paid only if earned, Were this suggestion of Mr. Vaughan approved by parliament, it would go far towards placing the fixed charges of Canadian National on a comparable basis with other roads in Canada and the United States. This is, however, a question for parliament and not one for consideration of the board.
The situation as it stands today is that the Canadian National Railways must earn sufficient net railway operating income to meet fixed charges, which, in 1947 amounted to $44,745,000. On the other hand the Canadian Pacific Railway Company only needs $18,000,0-00 for fixed charges.
The suggestion which Mr. Vaughan made in a statement before the board that the amount of $400,000,000 which the government had lent the railway for the purpose of repatriating securities should be placed on an income bond basis, that is, that the interest on this amount would be paid only if earned, seems to me a matter that the government should take under serious consideration.
In considering interest rates alone, and the difference in interest rates paid by the two companies, I find that in 1947 on capital borrowings bearing interest of 4 per cent or more the Canadian Pacific borrowed $10,700,000 at 4 per cent, while the Canadian National borrowed $128,000,000 at 5 per cent; $48,000,000 at 4-| per cent; $181,000,000 at 44 per cent and $46,000,000 at 4 per cent.
If the government would bring about refunding of the Canadian National debt to such a point where it would not be overly burdened, the need for increased freight rates would not be so great.
Speaking before the railway committee of the House of Commons on Monday, April 19, Mr. Vaughan said that the question of lowering

the burden of debt the line owes the government was constantly before the finance department; interest payments were entirely too high.
In the railways' application for higher rates they pointed to the great increases in wages paid employees. I believe it was yesterday that the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) drew to the attention of the house the wonderful progress which has been made in technological developments. He pointed to the fact that larger engines are hauling larger trains and larger boxcars, and that there are greater numbers of them. In that connection I should like to place a few figures on record. In 1922 there were 165,635 employees of all the railroads in Canada. During that year the railways carried 108,530,518 freight tons, or an average of 655-2 freight tons per employee. In 1946 they had 180,383 employees and carried 179,966,180 freight tons, or an average of 997-7 freight tons per employee. This represents an increase of about 52 per cent in freight tons per employee. I think that is something which has not thus far been brought to the attention of the house.
It has been suggested to me by different Canadian National employees that some discrimination exists against the Canadian National in the matter of handling government business. For instance, on October 11, 1945, 1.700 recruits were moved from Vancouver to Halifax on the Canadian Pacific railway, which required four trains of seventeen cars each. In giving me this information, a Canadian National employee had this to say:
Here we have the C.N.R. with a better grade, where one engine could handle each train, standing by while the C.P.R. requiring three engines to each train through the mountains, walks off with a rich haul. I cannot resist drawing this to your attention as it is a case of the C.P.R. getting the cream of the transportation business in every instance and our officials sit back apparently helpless because of the pressure from somewhere, I do not know.
In the northern part of my constituency, the Canadian Pacific have running rights over several Canadian National lines. My information, which I got from a source which I believe is reliable, is that the Canadian Pacific pick up loads all along the Canadian National line. I am also informed that mail travelling on the Canadian National destined to the west coast from Saskatoon is unloaded in Edmonton and reloaded on the Canadian Pacific route through Calgary. These are matters which I think should be investigated and, if found to be correct, rectified.
In 1947 estimates of the Post Office Department, I find that the Canadian Pacific received

Freight Rates
84,177,775 for mail carried, while the Canadian National received S3,756,489, or $421,286 less than that received by the Canadian Pacific. This means that the Canadian National receive 11 per cent less of moneys paid for carrying mail than did the Canadian Pacific.
I want to draw the attention of the house to the fact that the total mileage of the Canadian National Railways is 23,660 miles, while that of the Canadian Pacific Railway is 20,899 miles, giving to the Canadian National almost 13 per cent more miles than the Canadian Pacific, so that with 13 per cent more mileage than the Canadian Pacific the Canadian National receives 11 per cent less of the moneys paid by the government for carrying mail.
This situation is bad enough, but there is another type of discrimination, to which I should like to direct the attention of the government. This is something to which I have drawn attention before. Governments in the past have allowed the Canadian Pacific to run branch lines into districts adjacent to Canadian National lines. We all know that these lines go through districts which vary as to the kind of soil and in other respects. You can go into Saskatchewan and find many places where the Canadian National have built lines into fertile districts which are now tapped by the Canadian Pacific. The latter company is taking freight which I think should justifiably go to our own Canadian National.
The Minister of Transport is young and energetic. I think he should begin to take a greater interest in the Canadian National Railways and to see that this sort of discrimination is done away with.
During the period of the war the railways did very well and there was no talk of an increase in rates. This because they were able to carry on a two-way traffic and lots of it. But many times in the past those of us who come from the west have seen our farm products hauled away in mile-long trains loaded to capacity. We got very little for those products, with the result that we also saw mile-long trains coming back from eastern Canada consisting of empty boxcars. We should see to it that that condition never recurs, because if it does we shall have the railroads asking for another increase in freight rates.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon, member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). The minister has complained that many of the speeches made during this debate have been destructive in character, but I think the hon. member for Davenport made some good suggestions. One suggestion was that there should be greater production and the development of backward areas.
In offering a partial solution to this question of freight rates, I would suggest three main points for the government to consider. First, there should be a refinancing of the Canadian National debt structure and a reduction of the interest rate. Second, there should be planning for more traffic by increased production. Third, subsidies should be paid where necessary in connection with lines which are not productive and where the traffic is not sufficient to pay operating costs.
After this action has been taken, the board of transport commissioners, to which I think some new blood should be added, should then carry out the provisions of the Railway Act, which states that there should be equality as to tolls with respect to all traffic carried under substantially similar circumstances and conditions and that no toll shall be charged which unjustly discriminates between different localities.
Mr. -ROBERT FAIR (Battle River): Mr. Speaker, I shall delay the house for only a few minutes because the case for this group has been placed before the house and the government earlier in the debate. We consider that it was good business to state our case and let it rest. This morning, as well as during the past weeks since this freight rate increase has been in effect, I have received a number of complaints. I should like to bring two of these to the attention of the house.
The first was received from a merchant in a small town near the Saskatchewan border who complains about express rates from Edmonton to his town. On April 3 he received from Edmonton a shipment of two boxes weighing 55 pounds for which he paid 42 cents. On April 10 he received a similar two boxes weighing 54 pounds for which he was billed 81 cents, or practically a 100 per cent increase. We have been given to understand that only a 21 per cent increase was authorized. One week later, on April 17, he received another shipment weighing 52 pounds for which he was billed 80 cents. This party has written me and he wants an explanation which I cannot give him. If the minister can give me an answer I will pass it on to this merchant. He and many others are really peeved about this increase in freight rates which has been granted without having the discriminatory features of the freight rate structure remuv- J.
I received a letter this morning from the Edmonton chamber of commerce. This contains some suggestions which I should like to place on the record. Their letter reads:
It is the opinion of this chamber that such an inquiry should be conducted by an independent
Freight Rates

tribunal, in the nature of a Toyal commission, and this chamber has so advocated for the past year and a half. In so advocating, the chamber does not desire to express lack of confidence in the board of transport commissioners, but desires to point out that what may in some rejects be an appeal from the findings of a quasi judicial body should not be referred to the same body. Furthermore, the chamber feels the inquiry should be by well qualified men, versed in the field of commerce and economics who would be unhampered in any way by the statutory restrictions by which the board of transport commissioners has heretofore been hedged about.
The chamber has been advocating, and still advocates, the appointment of a commission of the prestige and influence of the Rowell-Sirois commission because the chamber feels the question of freight rates is the single most important matter facing the Canadian economy at the present time.
Skipping two or three paragraphs, I quote again:
... it would seem unfortunate that the findings of any such inquiry should be anticipated by the implementation- of the present 21 per cent increase, and the chamber considers it to be in the interests of Canada that the findings of the board of transport commissioners be deferred until the new inquiry has had an- opportunity of hearing evidence, fully considering matters and reporting to the government of the day.
In the view of this chamber it would be in the public interest, if necessary, to protect independent railways from operating losses by governmental subsidy while the commission conducts its study.
That is the exact stand which was taken by this group when our position was placed before the house some days ago. I want to endorse these suggestions fully, as does my group, and commend them to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the government.

I hope that I and all other members will profit by this incident. May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to add a few personal words. Ever since I entered this chamber in 1943, in my conscience before God, I have not said or done anything in this house that was out of order; and even if I did not honour you personally as I do, I should still honour the office you hold and endeavour to conduct myself in an honourable and upright manner in this house.
The amendment moved by my leader the hon. member for Rosetown^Biggar (Mr. Cold-well), as I was saying before I was interrupted by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier)-and if I may be permitted to say so, our whole difficulty this evening has come from the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner)-was moved to persuade the government that, for the time being, they should withhold the
Freight Rates

application of the order of the board of transport commissioners. I could show how this freight rate increase will affect my constituency and the province from which I come, and, going beyond the confines of that province, how it will affect other parts of this dominion, but I shall not weary the house this evening when apparently the members are in such a hurry to do something which I believe they will regret before many years are over.
I received my early education in the southern states, where I was bom, in the union to the south of us. In the first part of that education the British form of government was not spoken of in any too glowing terms, but, having come to this country as a young lad and continued my education here, I was very soon impressed by the parliamentary system of government that prevails throughout the British empire. Following the admonitions of my father, I endeavoured to study that system, and the more I studied it, the more firmly I came to the conclusion that we had in this country a form of government that was well adapted to accomplishing everything we desired and that it was one that should be furthered and encouraged.
As one goes on through life, things sometimes occur, and possibly something occurred this evening, to check one's firm belief in something that he admires and loves. But all this while, Mr. Speaker, I have believed and still do believe in our parliamentary system of government, and one of our rights under that system is the right of appeal, even to the foot of the throne, if necessary. The appeal from the board's decision would go before the ministers who are His Majesty's advisers.
On a question such as this which affects the people of this country so vitally, we hear a great deal said about the need for national unity. I plead with the ministers on the treasury benches, who are seemingly determined to have this order go into effect before even the appeal against it can be heard, to withhold the imposition of the order until those provinces which have registered notice of their intention to appeal may be heard. On Saturday the premiers of seven of the nine provinces are to present their case to the government, and I think it would be only fair and proper for this house to defer the vote on the amendment moved by my leader until next week, until that appeal is heard. One way of doing that would be for the members from the west and the maritime provinces to continue this debate, but personally I think there is a much better way. All that this house has to do is to agree to adjourn this debate until some time next week. In the

meantime we can go on with our other work. I shall make the proper motion in this respect in a moment. Because of the anxiety that has been shown by hon. members on the Liberal benches for us to get on with the business of the house, I am sure that they will support the motion I am about to make. I think it will be better for all concerned and in the interests of national unity for the government to go on with the other business of the house and give the premiers of the seven provinces an opportunity to present their case. Therefore I hope they will support my motion. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. McKay):
That this debate be now adjourned.

Thank you, Little Chicago. You will get your own dose back one of these days, and I will do my share of it. If you do not know what courtesy is, we on this side of the house can teach you.
The gentlemen to whom I refer, who have participated so splendidly in this fight in past years, are the late Senator McGeer and the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). The late Senator McGeer was untiring in his efforts to obtain a better deal for the province of British Columbia; and I dare to think in my own mind that his interest in this problem went much deeper than the mere legal emolument he may have received for his services. Standing by his side year after year, tilting a brave lance, was the hon. member for New Westminster.
As I said a few moments ago, I am not an expert on this freight rate issue, but I do know something of the harmful effect this 21 per cent increase will have on the lives of the people of my constituency. In the Kootenays we produce huge quantities of goods and commodities:	coal, lumber, ores, fruit, dairy

produce and wheat. I am sure it would not hurt the house to learn that in my constituency, in the Creston valley area, lives Mrs. Amy Kelsey, who grew in that district wheat which won first prize at the Chicago exhibition and made her the wheat queen of North America.
When I speak of freight rates I am not speaking specifically for those larger producing interests, though naturally they are concerned over this 21 per cent increase. I am thinking particularly of the fruit growers of my constituency, the men who pack from two thousand to six or eight thousand boxes of fruit each season. These are the people who now are being over-burdened with this 21 per cent increase in freight rates; and I want to tell the members of this house that it does not matter whether these growers are Liberals, Conservatives, C.C.F. or what have you, every last one of them is opposed to this increase. I believe it has already been pointed out in this debate that this increase will cost the fruit growers of British Columbia, particularly the tree fruit growers, a round million dollars extra in distributive transportation costs.
I have been amused the last few days, believe it or not, at the eagerness with which hon. members on the government benches, who are not here now-and if it was the noisy crowd we can well do without them-have been calling for the vote. They have all been so eager to have the vote: "Question; question!" they yell, every time an opposition member gets up to speak. I would remind them that that eagerness stems from the time the party caucus was held immediately after the moving of the amendment to which we are now speaking. The press all across the country carried headlines, "Government Threatened". Then after getting something of the news which came out of the party caucus, and after hearing various members on the government benches speak their piece, members who might well have been expected to bolt on this issue, the press, after hearing them say that they would vote to sustain the government, began, of course, to change its tune. Then we began to see new headlines: "Government Weathers Storm".
I venture to point out there are times when even the press of this country makes mistakes. And I am not so sure that the government has weathered the storm. My message to the government is this. Just because you may win this vote, do not pat yourselves on the back. This storm is just beginning. Instead of patting yourselves on the back, my advice would be to prepare to meet the deluge-because you will have to meet it if these things go on.

No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.

Mr. P.E. WRIGHT (Melfort): Mr. Speaker, it had not been my intention to take part in this debate; but since I have seen that the government did not want the debate adjourned, but wished to see it carried on for the rest of this evening at least, I thought it my duty to take part in it.
Coming from western Canada, where we are particularly interested in the recent increase, because of its effect on our basic industry out there, I felt that as a farmer representative in the house I should have something to say about it. The implementing of this 21 per cent increase without first removing the inimical and unjust freight rates structure is probably the worst feature of the present situation. It leads to discontent and to a feeling of rank injustice in a great many parts of our dominion. This is something which any government in Canada should try to avoid at all costs.
If the government had agreed to the postponement for six months of the implementation of this 21 per cent increase, until the matter had been placed before the board of transport commissioners, and some equalization in the freight rates structure of Canada agreed upon, I do not think there would have been the feeling that there is throughout Canada today with regard to it. I can assure hon. members of the Liberal party that they have not a majority in the country so far as the feeling of discrimination in connection with this matter is concerned. There are many people all across Canada who consider that the 21 per cent increase at this time is unjust. I believe that it is unjust, and that the railways are making a mistake. They spend large sums of money every year to create better relations with the public. I do not think they could have done anything which would have more impressed the public with their genuineness than by having asked that this 21 per cent increase be deferred until there had been an equalization of the freight rates structure. It would have been good business on the part of the railway companies to have made that suggestion, even though the government or the board of transport commissioners were prepared immediately to give the increase.
Many examples have been given of just what this 21 per cent increase means, especially as it affects small shippers. The discrimination is much greater as it applies to people in outlying areas who cannot collect their produce for large shipments. Figures were given here both by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) and the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Argue) showing this discrimination as between large and small

shippers. This is particularly true with respect to eggs and cream. In many cases the increase is not 21 per cent, it is 50 and 100 per cent.
When the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) spoke he gave figures to indicate that these increases would mean only a small increase in the prices of butter, tea, coffee and other articles of consumption in Canada, but the figures he gave did not show the whole picture. The increase in the freight on these articles when moving into centres for distribution was not included in his figures. When you consider those increases you will find it amounts to as much as two or three cents more for a pound of butter.
Either the producer or the consumer must pay that increase. If the producer pays it, it means there is less spending power in the hands of the producer. If the consumer pays it, it means a higher cost of living in Canada. I do not think the government should be doing anything today to increase the cost of living. Surely they realize that that is something about which the people are today protesting right across Canada. They also are protesting the inflationary effects of this increase in the freight rates.
This increase of 21 per cent is pyramided two or three times before the article being shipped reaches the final producer or consumer. The minister did not given any examples of what this increase means in connection with prices of binders, tractors, farm machinery and all those things entering into the cost of production. The increase of 21 per cent means an increase of from $30 to $70 in the cost of many implements. That is not a small item at a time when prices have been increased several times during the last year or two.
This increase of 21 per cent in freight rates will be a serious blow to the livestock industry in western Canada. There is not only an increase of 21 per cent in the freight from the local point to Winnipeg; there will be a greater effect through the fact that the Winnipeg market will be lower in relationship to the eastern markets. Over a period of time the Winnipeg market price is based on the eastern price plus freight to eastern Canada. The Winnipeg market is generally that much lower and that increase will mean another general lowering of livestock prices in western Canada. That will be an important thing at a time when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is asking for more bacon and an increased production in our livestock and

dairy industries. The government is passing legislation which will discourage that increase in production.
There will also be an increased demand from western Canada that the government absorb the freight on livestock shipped to the eastern markets. The government now pay the freight on coarse grains from the head of the lakes to eastern Canada, with which policy I agree, but if the government are prepared to do that they should be prepared to pay the freight on livestock and dairy products from western Canada to the eastern markets. As I say, this 21 per cent increase will mean more pressure on the government to do that very thing.
If the government pays the freight on coarse grains for the feeding of livestock it is only fair that the livestock producer in western Canada should have the freight paid on the products he ships to the eastern markets.
I should like to point out another example of discrimination not connected with agriculture. The freight rate on a cord of pulpwood shipped from a point ten miles from Hudson Bay Junction to Fort Frances is $2.90, whereas, when the same cord of wood is shipped to Churchill practically the same distance, the rate is $13 a cord or $212 a car. Recently there was a demand for poplar logs to be shipped through Churchill to Great Britain and Europe for the making of matches. When the exporters inquired about freight rates on logs going through Churchill they found this discriminatory freight rate structure, and the result was that it was impossible for them to take advantage of that market.
Where it cost $212 to ship a carload of pulp-wood to Churchill it cost only $46.40 to ship the same car to Fort Frances, the same distance. What does the 21 per cent increase amount to in those cases? In the case of the car going to Churchill the increase amounts to $42, whereas in the case of the car going to Fort Frances it amounts to only $10. The increase is four times as large in the one case for a car travelling the same distance.
It is discrimination like that to which people object. It is impossible to develop industry in western Canada, for export markets for some of the things we can produce. Why accentuate that discrimination by a 21 per cent flat increase? It is absolute nonsense to talk of equality and equity when the government are prepared to go ahead and implement that type of increase before equalizing our freight rates. I do not think there would be much objection, and there certainly would

not be as much as there has been to the increase if the government had done something to remove these inequities.
I would say that from every point of view delay in implementing the increase was justified. From the point of view of better relationships between the railways and the public, and this is of particular importance to the railways themselves which have to meet competition today by road and air transport, and from the point of view of increasing the already high living costs in Canada, this 21 per cent freight rate increase is entirely unjustified at this time. Its pyramiding effect will increase the cost of living and be the cause of further inflation. I therefore submit that even at this late date the government should defer implementing this increase in freight rates until at least some equalization has been made in our freight rate structure, either by the board of transport commissioners or by some other body set up for that purpose.

When you go back into history and read the story of how the railways came into being you realize that it was an epic of achievement. The credit should go, not to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, but to the pioneers in this country who backed their confidence in it with their dollars, by gifts to the company, by loans, by bond guarantees, by tremendous grants of land particularly throughout our prairies and in British Columbia, by tax exemptions, by special concessions from governments, dominion, provincial and municipal, to make the Canadian Pacific railway the tie that bound Canada from coast to coast.
It is fallacious to think of the Canadian Pacific railway in any sense as a privately owned public utility. By some freak of financial strategy, shall we say, though some people might call it business acumen, a group of people banded themselves together as a corporation and extracted concessions from the public domain, with the result that a railway worth originally several tens or, at the most,

to the dominion government on behalf of a reconsideration of the freight rate structure, have been as long suffering as they have.
In the report of the board of transport commissioners authorizing or concurring in a 21 per cent freight rate increase, the word "discrimination" often appears. The board admit that there is discrimination in rates as between the central provinces and the remaining portion of the Dominion of Canada. They say that there is evidence of discrimination but there is no evidence of unjust discrimination. One of the most amazing peculiarities of our English language is that of combining a pair of contradictory phrases. To me discrimination seems to be the ultimate. The board of transport commissioners, however, are willing to agree that discrimination exists in our freight rate structure, but they say it has not been shown to their satisfaction that that discrimination is unjust discrimination.
It has been mentioned in this debate that the comparatively sparsely settled sections of Canada, the prairie provinces, have contributed 65 per cent of the net revenues of the Canadian Pacific at a time when the more thickly populated sections of central Canada, with much greater traffic, have been able to contribute only 35 per cent of the net revenues of that railway company. The very fact that on a population basis we contributed from the prairies sixfold the profit to the railway companies that a more richly endowed Ontario and Quebec contributed, it seems to me, speaks for the callous disregard of the sense of public responsibility that a public utility ought to have. We in the west contributed equally if not more than eastern Canada toward the construction of the railway lines that cross this country. Should we go on in perpetuity paying disproportionate transportation costs because of the distance goods have to travel to get to our provinces? Must we go on paying on a mileage basis 15 per cent, as is stated to be the average in the differential between the rate in eastern Canada and that on the prairies, or in many cases running many times that, just because we have not the ballot power, shall I say, to cause the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) to adopt a more open-minded view with regard to justice for all parts of this federal union?

I have lived in the west a good deal, and I know perfectly well that there is a need for the equalization of freight rates. That instruction has been g!'"'ri to the board of transport commissioners and that equalization will be made just as soon as possible.
The other issue is, to me, also clear. I have been a strong advocate of increased pensions and increased pay for the workers. If these freight rates had not been increased, I would not have been a bit surprised if there had been a strike on the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. We talk about serving two masters. I do not know whether there is much difference between doing that and being on the horns of a dilemma. I think we must be fair. These workers ' on the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National and other railroads have a right to consideration. Out of these increased freight rates they will get their share, and it is our duty to see that they do.
There is another thing I should like to say. When we come toward the end of a session, we often hear the criticism that not enough time is being spent on the estimates. I think if we cut down our speeches on freight rates we would have more time to spend on the estimates.

I do not want to take up much time in this debate, Mr. Speaker. I think it has been carried on long enough. I am quite aware that we must have an increase in freight rates, but I want to see a fair increase. The other day the minister told us that he had a board of transport commissioners who were experts in the handling of freight rates. I want to tell this house that in Canada since July we have had an increase in freight rates of 10 per cent on all shipments to the United States. Before the United States interstate commerce commission authorized that increase, the railways of Canada were allowed to increase their freight rates, on the mileage haul over Canadian territory, by 10 per cent from July on, and by 20 per cent from October on. It costs $207 to carry a carload of potatoes from New Brunswick to Windsor, Ontario; and it costs $378 to carry it to Detroit, Michigan. That is $171 extra for carrying it across the river to Detroit. Does the minister call that fair?
I call that discrimination of the worst kind, and I do not think he has many experts in the board of transport commissioners. They allowed the Canadian railways to charge the increase in freight rates that the United States railroads made before the interstate commerce commission even authorized it. I ask the minister:	Is that not a fact?

I was quoting from the amendment which is now before the house. I repeat that, since this amendment calls attention to the fact that the imposition of the 21 per cent increase in freight rates is inimical to the best interests of the people of Canada, that in itself opens up a wide field for discussion. If it were not that I am going to catch a train I should like very much tonight to take advantage of the breadth of that amendment and deal with some of the freight rates, not the inequalities but just how the increases will affect the poorer people. I imagine many speakers have already done that, but I should like very much to have done it over again, because I do not think we can tell the story too often.
Let me say at once that the mere increase in freight rates does not concern me, beyond this, that I believe our freight rates should be sufficient to carry the services the railways must give the people of this country. Everyone will admit at once that our railway system is indispensable. It must be made to run efficiently, in the interests of the economic system of the country; but, sir, in my opinion we could do that and still reduce freight rates in the west, because the basis upon which the freight rates have been struck is inequitable, unjustifiably so. I presume the board-it used to be the board of railway commissioners but its new baptismal name is the board of transport commissioners-in hearing the evidence of those opposed to the increase, came to its judgment on the basis of past practices. It appears to me that it never occurred to the board there was anything the matter with freight rates, that the only thing it had in mind was whether the rates were to be higher or lower, on the same basis as in the past.
I think that was a very careless way to consider the matter, but I repeat that I do not think the board is to blame. I think the blame must rest on this government and past governments. I believe those who first set up the board are also to blame. In my opinion the board was brought into being to protect the Canadian Pacific. I do not believe we would have had it at all had we not been forced to take over the bankrupt railways. Those railways were taken over, not because the government of that day loved public ownership or wanted to institute a great

Freight Rates
national transportation system. They were taken over because they were bankrupt; the country was at war, and the services of the railways were required. Certain plans were made for running them; and one of the things that was to be understood from the beginning, apparently, was that nothing was to interfere with the supremacy of the Canadian Pacific; that if it should be found the Canadian National could haul more goods through the mountains or across the prairies with the same amount of power, or could travel faster and carry passengers to the coast in ten or twelve hours less time than the Canadian Pacific, then that was to be regarded as unfair competition. Therefore one of the duties of this board was to lay down the time schedules for passenger traffic.

Before I was interrupted I was discussing the matter of the function of the board in regulating the supposed competition between the two railways. The fact of the matter is that they regulate it so that there is practically no competition. That leads to the need for higher freight rates.
Perhaps one of the most striking speeches made during this debate was that of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). I believe he gave some interesting data, and I would commend what he said to hon. members. I would also refer to the speech of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka), who put on Hansard figures which I think it would be difficult for anyone to gainsay. May I sum up in a word or two what he said on this particular point? He went on to show, quoting the actual figures of the Canadian Pacific, that the population of the west was, I believe, a little less than a third of the entire population of the country; and yet, according to those figures, those people pay two-thirds of the revenues of that railway. I would ask the Minister of Transport to put that in his mind, and think about it. Then he will understand why it is that people who represent the west are aroused on a question of this kind. If it is desired to retain unity in this country and to prevent spiteful feeling and anger arising in one part of the country against another part, then this basic injustice must be removed. And we must take the opportunity now afforded to make this matter plain to the minister, to the government and to parliament itself.
The hon. member who spoke immediately preceding me made reference to the workers, that their wages were implicated, and that but for the granting of this increase a strike might have taken place. I hope the hon. member knows better than that. I think it has been made clear by the representatives of both railways, and by the representatives of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in rebuttal that the rates of wages of employees

of the railways were not conditional upon the decision of the board with respect to this matter.
Let me say to the hon. member that we are not, by any means, opposing the increasing of wages. I would say for myself that I am not opposing the increase in freight rates as such, because, as I have said, I believe that we can increase freight rates sufficiently to carry the service and to reduce them west of the great lakes, provided that we find an equitable, honest and defensible basis upon which to strike our freight rates.
I am sorry I have to stop at this point, because this has been only an introduction to what I had wanted to say. I hope, however, that what I have said will be noticed by the administration. And since they are so anxious to cultivate free enterprise; since they are so married to the principle of competition, then I am asking that the Canadian National Railways be given their head; that there be no more curbing of those railways, that they be allowed to run freight as cheaply as they can run it, and to carry passengers as quickly and as cheaply as they can do so, and we shall very soon bring down freight rates.
