subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the last occasion I spoke in this debate I made out a case, satisfactory at least to myself and to many others, to show that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had not made out a case for itself, on the facts before the board of transport commissioners, for any increase in freight rates. I intend to dilate on that tonight.
Obviously the Canadian Pacific has not made out a case for increased freight rates, and these freight rate increases should not have been given to it. I wish to quote here one of the basic fallacies which I find permeating this judgment of the board of transport commissioners. At page 10 they say:
As earlier mentioned the present application of the railway association, which was made in October, 1946, was predicated, upon declining operating revenues, and increasing operating expenses brought about by higher wage rates and increased costs of materials.
That assumption has been proven to be entirely wrong, and the facts of the matter are clearly before the people of Canada. Let us consider the situation as it exists this year.
The application is predicated upon the decline in operating revenues. Yet we find that the gross revenues for January and February of this year for the Canadian Pacific are something like $49,000,000 as compared with $44,000,000 last year, or an increase of about $5,000,000, or 10-8 per cent. It is true that operating expenses also increased. They were $49,442,000 in 1947, whereas last year they were $45,233,000. But operating expenses increased by only 9-3 per cent. So that we find that last year, whereas the Canadian Pacific in those two months made a loss of $839,000, this year their loss was reduced to $230,000. Obviously there is no case here for having increased freight rates on the basis of declining revenues, when the revenues are obviously increased.

Freight Rates
Furthermore, as of April 10, carloadings have increased this year to 421,630 as compared with 410,379 last year. If the government is going to support the judgment of the board on the basis that we can expect declining revenues, then the government will find itself within the year in a most invidious position. Declining revenue suggests that there will be some economic recession. If there is to be economic recession there will be unemployment. Within a year we shall have an election; is the government going to the country on the basis that it expects unemployment? Certainly not. The government will go to the country on the basis of expected full employment. If such is the case, then we can expect that Canadian Pacific revenues will continue to increase.
I should like to return to some figures which I mentioned briefly on the last occasion on which I spoke and which are germane to the debate tonight. An allowance was granted to the Canadian Pacific by the board of transport commissioners for surplus and additions and betterments, totalling some $15,235,000. It is possible that the Canadian Pacific, having been freely awarded this additional surplus, will spend the money to buy better equipment. If they buy equipment they are going to depreciate it, which means that this asset will be charged twice against freight rates, and not just once.
We have the extraordinary position where the board and the government apparently agree that there should be allowed to the Canadian Pacific a total of 821,310,000 for dividends, $15,787,000 for fixed charges and $15,235,000 as an allowance for surplus, or a total of some $52,000,000. That is what the government and the board believe the Canadian Pacific should have to play about with after its expenses have been met. That includes dividends of five per cent to the ordinary shareholders. However, as I argued, out of this allowance for surplus it is possible that the ordinary shareholders may get another five per cent. But the board and the government do not include a total of $22,000,000 of other income which the Canadian Pacific is able to earn from investments. In other words, the position of the government is that they are quite content to see the Canadian Pacific in a position where it can possibly pay out dividends of as high as 20 per cent to its shareholders, while the people of Canada have to pay the shot.
It was brought out in evidence that, since their inception, United States railroads have earned approximately four per cent on their
investment. I suggest that that percentage is quite large enough for the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific. If such is the case, then they do not need this great surplus which has been given to them. Among the arguments which were advanced before the board was a fantastic statement by the railway association of Canada that the railroad companies were in a unique and perilous position. I have already dealt with that.
We also had Mr. George Walker, vicepresident of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, stating that that company was in urgent need of financial aid. Then Mr. Liddy of the Canadian Pacific spoke of the company's perilous financial position. Mr. Crump referred to the critical financial position, while Mr. Unwin referred to the disquieting financial position. Again we find those words echoed by the chairman of the board of transport commissioners, and I quote from the judgment as follows:
A close analysis of the current operating revenues of Canadian railways indicates that lower levels may, perhaps, reasonably be expected.
Of course that is an unmitigated example of soothsaying at its very worst. It has nothing whatsoever to do with the facts of the situation. As I say, the facts are infinitely better than one would suspect from this judgment which has been given to us. On the basis of those facts, I should like the minister to answer some questions which I am going to pose to him. It has been argued that the Canadian Pacific is in a difficult financial position, a perilous financial position and a unique position. I think "unique' is probably the proper word.
Does the minister deny for a moment the increase in operating revenue figures which I have presented to the house? Does he deny that since 1939, according to the Canadian Pacific balance sheet-the whole case for increased freight rates was based on that- the company has retired all its six per cent bonds, all its five per cent bonds and all its four and a half per cent bonds? Does that suggest that this railroad is in a perilous financial position?
Does the minister deny the excellent cash position of the Canadian Pacific in its last-balance sheet, which showed cash of some $42,644,000. Does he deny that the Canadian Pacific owns dominion securities totalling $31,667,000? Does that indicate that this railroad is suffering from a critical financial position? If it does not, then why has it been given this quite unmerited increase in freight rates?

Does the minister deny that since 1939 the funded debt of the Canadian Pacific had been decreased by .$153 million; that is, from $228 million to $75 million? Does that suggest an urgent need of financial aid? Does the minister deny that the Canadian Pacific has increased its reserves from $92 million to $380 million? Does he deny that its profit and loss balance in its balance sheet has increased from $141 million to $279 million? Does he deny that its working capital has been increased by $48 million over 1939? Do those figures suggest for a moment that the Canadian Pacific is in a perilous financial position, or that it is in a critical financial position?
Does the minister deny that the Canadian Pacific has in its balance sheet stock of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company shown at a book value of $8,412,000, whereas the market value today is in the neighbourhood of $150 million? Does the minister deny that that is an example of hidden reserves in the balance sheet of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company? Does the minister deny that from 1940 to 1946 the Canadian Pacific made expenditures on railroad property of $123 million? Does he deny that it invested in leased lines, out of funds from its corporate operations, $11,500,000? Does that suggest a disquieting financial position?
Does the minister deny that the Canadian Pacific made capital expenditure on steamships, hotels and communications of some $18,000,000 between 1940 and 1946? Does he deny that it invested in stocks and bonds of controlled and other companies and advanced to subsidiaries some $20,000,000 during those years? Does he deny that it spent out of its funds for organization of the Soo line some $7,000,000? Does the minister deny that it established a steamship replacement fund of $39,000,000 during those years? Is there any sign of a perilous financial position when one considers the reserves which have been created?
Does the minister deny that this company, which is in such straitened circumstances, paid out interest during those years totalling $150,000,000, and that it paid out in income and other taxes $120,000,000? Does the minister deny that this poverty-stricken corporation paid out in dividends over those years $91,000,000, or that it established a deferred maintenance reserve of $25,000,000? Now and again the vernacular is almost vulgar, but sometimes it is quite expressive. I intend to use the vernacular in this case and say that the Canadian Pacific is simply lousy with hidden reserves.
There can be no question about it at all, this company does not need the increase in freight rates which has been granted to it. There can 
be no question at all about its being able to pay quite easily, without any increase in freight rates, the wages which its employees demand and that it can continue to do so for another two years. There is no reason why this company could not pay out of its accumulated surplus and reserves the pensions which its employees need. Rut the company has no intention of doing that. All our attention must be concentrated entirely on freight rates. These increased freight rates are absolutely inequitable and unjust and I can see no reason or sense for their having been granted at all.

No, I will not dispense. I want to get this on the record so that I shall be sure that I do not stray from it. The first part of the amendment reads:
this house is of the opinion that the failure of the government to defer the imposition of the increases in freight rates recently authorized by the board of transport commissioners is inimical to the best interests of the people of Canada . . .
That is the first part, and I propose, first, to endeavour to prove to the government and their side of the house that that is indeed the fact, that this measure is inimical to the best interests of the people of Canada. In endeavouring to produce evidence to prove my point,
I shall show how generous the people of Canada have already been to the railway companies, and I hope that my evidence will be convincing enough to conjure up in the government some bowels of compassion for the ordinary everyday working citizen. Then, if I have time, after I have proved that point,
I shall deal with the second part of the amendment, which reads:
further this house is of the opinion that the government should reconsider this matter and take action to prevent the proposed increases from coming into effect at this time.
I shall endeavour to adduce arguments that will be, I hope, reasonably convincing to the government why they should undertake that.
In order to deal with the first part of the amendment and do what I said I would do, that is, show that the people of Canada have already been generous to the railway companies, I am going to quote from the public

Freight Rates
accounts of the Dominion of Canada for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1947. In part III, at page 3, appears a "Statement of Assistance given to railways by the Dominion of Canada to March 31, 1947." If hon. members will listen carefully they will see that the people of Canada have already been very generous with both the railroads.
First, let me deal with the Canadian National, and in giving these figures I want to give the house some idea of the history of these railways, not what I have read in books but what I have learned from actual work in the railway and lumber camps in the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific through the mountains to Prince Rupert and the Transcontinental in northern Ontario; and from the point of view of one who has swung an axe or skinned a horse or driven the rivers, I think no one in the House of Commons has a closer knowledge of the building of the railways than I have. When I remember the things that went on, the graft and corruption by the contractors, Foley, Welsh and Stewart and the various subcontractors, it is easy to understand the tremendous capital overhead of the Canadian National, which I have already mentioned in another debate in this house.
When you remember wooden bridges, with 137 to 150 bents being built according to specifications-and I know something about the building of wooden bridges, Mr. Speaker- and then the whole gang of men having to come back within two months and cut down every single bent and eighteen inches off every pile in that bridge and lower every cap and make new guard rails simply because of carelessness in construction or because some lumber company wanted to sell piling that was a little longer than the specifications called for; when you remember that the approaches to many bridges cost many dollars more because of the extra yardage put in to make extra profits for contractors and subcontractors, and when you follow that right through, you begin to have some idea why the road is overcapitalized at the present time. When you go up through northern Ontario, north of Fort William by Sioux Lookout and in all that country where O'Brien, Fowler and McDougall had their contracts, and where trainload after trainload of gravel wras dumped into almost bottomless muskeg, until finally it did hit the bottom and then came up and spread out for half a mile on each side, and when you consider that that was done when even in those days there were better ways of engineering, it is not surprising that the people of Canada had to make the gifts they did.
I mention these facts, Mr. Speaker, to prove my contention that the people of Canada have given enough in this way to the bondholders of the railways, and it is time now that the people of Canada got some protection themselves. I contend that the granting of this freight rate increase is inimical to the best interests of the people of Canada on these grounds. I could cite instance after instance. I could tell you about hacking ties with a broad axe for eight and nine and ten cents a lie, which were culled by the inspectors, and the culled ties were then put into the right of way for the rails to go on. I could give you instance after instance right down to the bootlegging of rotgut liquor if you want me to. Hon. gentlemen opposite who are grumbling never bad a grub-hoe in their hands I suppose, and never used dynamite and could not run a wheelbarrow if it had directions written on the handle. I will try to finish my speech early enough for some of these hon. gentlemen on your right, Mr. Speaker, to get up and speak if they have any objection to what I am saying.

speechtext:
However, Mr. Speaker, I want to get to the third column in this book, because this is the amount written off. This is one of the straight gifts of the Canadian people. The amount written off was the whole $44,179,077.92 of cash subsidies, and the total amount of deficits and operating expenditures of $498,454,367. Then there were loans. Loans are assumed to be something that you get back eventually. Unfortunately I have a few small loans like that, that I am not optimistic about, but that is the hope we have when we make a loan. Of course, when we borrow we hope we shall not have to pay the loan back, but if we are private citizens we usually have to, but not if we are a railway. If we are a railway under the government's wing we are pretty sure that we shall be forgiven some of our financial trespasses.
There were loans for capital expenditures and deficits of $733,592,151. There were loans for betterments of and repairs to railway equipment, no doubt getting new brass handles on

the diningroom car doors and things like that, of $1,183,592. Then railway equipment purchased and sold to the railway, under a hire-purchase agreement, of $91,872,555. I am omitting all cents here because there is not much sense in this whole matter when we come to look it over.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: Will the hon. member permit one question? I am very much interested in these figures. These loans were all government operations; in other words, socializing the railways. That is it, is it not? .

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with that question, and I could very extensively, but I know Your Honour would not permit me to get outside of the place that I prescribed for myself tonight. I do not want to incur the wrath of Your Honour, because you have always been good to me and I propose to treat you with the respect that you deserve; therefore I cannot answer my hon. friend now.

speechtext: You cannot.

speechtext:
I can answer it, but I will not answer it at the present time; I will put it that way.
There were temporary loans and advances, including loans made in connection with the government's relief program, of $1,391,388,526. The amount repaid, transferred, or discharged amounts to $911,940,510, and the amount written off is $263,456,953, a nice little gift paid to bondholders who, generally speaking, in this day and age do nothing to earn any of that at all, and are simply the heirs or successors of the people of the past. There is a considerable amount of that sum outstanding, over a billion dollars.
We then come down to the guarantees, loans guaranteed as to principal and interest by the dominion government, $1,314,515,436, and loans guaranteed as to interest only by the dominion government $216,207,141, or a total of $1,530,722,578, of which amount there was repaid, transferred or discharged, $995,307,235. The balance outstanding amounts to $535,415,342.
Then we have sundry assistance. Usually, when you are secretary of a small concern like an agricultural society, a co-operative association or something of that kind, when you make your financial statement at the end of the year you have a few little expenditures which are shown; maybe $2.75 or even $10.15. You put them in-as sundries because they may represent teaspoons that were lost when you had your annual meeting with a banquet or something of that sort. But when you get sundries to the extent of $58,358,242, that is -a sizeable piece of coin to give away.

speechtext: Order. I suppose the remarks made just now by the hon. member who has the floor are for the purpose of proving that we should have an increase in freight rates, although I am not so sure about that.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: You are correct in that supposition, Mr. Speaker. I am trying to prove that the increase is inimical to the best interests of the people of Canada; and as I stated before, in trying to prove my case I wanted to show that the people of Canada had already been generous enough with the railway companies and the bondholders of the railway companies and that there should be no further call for another $71,000,000 increase; that is the sum which the increased freight rates will amount to, so I am told. That is the point I am trying to make. As I said, by a recital of these tremendous figures I was hoping that I could arouse the compassion of some of my honourable and good-natured looking friends who sit on the treasury benches.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: But you failed.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
That was my purpose anyway in doing that.
I now want to come to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. It has had most generous treatment. I want to point out that I support the things wThich were said by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) when he was here. The Canadian Pacific has had entirely too much influence on the operation of the Canadian National all through the picture, both when the Canadian National was privately owned and since it has become a government institution. I think that is a regrettable situation.
When the Canadian Pacific was being built, we know there was difficulty, and we understand that there was a good deal of risk-capital involved. We know they were to go across what at that time were empty, or practically empty, prairies; and no one knew for sure that they would actually be productive. In order to recompense them to some extent- in fact, to recompense them to quite an extent-they were made a gift of 32,848,477 acres of land, according to this statement. With that they were given the mineral rights in a tremendous amount, if not all those acres, some of which mineral rights they have used to convert into tremendous wealth
Freight Rates

for the Canadian Pacific shareholders. This does not appear in the financial statement of the railroad and is not used, so far as I know, in paying the operating costs. Nevertheless the gift was made to them to recompense them for the risk they were taking in going across that wild country, as it was at that time.
It would appear that the government should accept this argument, that this railway company, having been given all those gifts, from there on should be subject to competition from any other transportation company which may appear on the scene. But instead of that, we have found that, in spite of the gifts to the Canadian National and in spite of the gifts to the Canadian Pacific, both of them now want to gouge the public more and more, instead of getting down to a basis of proving which one can operate most economically and most successfully in the interests of the Canadian people and still take care of their capital costs, pay decent wages and provide proper working conditions for the people who work on them.
Time does not allow me to go much farther with that particular part of my argument.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Go ahead.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: I could give a great deal more along that line.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Go ahead.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: I am simply trying to get the government to see the point of view that we have, that there is no excuse for their allowing the railways such a gift as that.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: You are not going to blame the rest for that.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
I am trying to prove my point. The hon. member for Kings (Mr. Grant) can have his fun with the Tory member for Queens (Mr. McLure) at some other time. I think I have already brought forward some fairly substantial evidence to support my point.
I want now to turn to the second part of the amendment which reads:
. . . further this house is of the opinion that the government should reconsider this matter and take action to prevent the proposed increases from coming into effect at this time.
There is only one appeal which a person can make to a body of people in authority for something of that kind. One must appeal to their reason and their generosity. I want to remind this government that, aside entirely from partisan political considerations, they have enjoyed-even from those who do not

support them politically-loyal support in Canadian policies from the people across this country. Right through the war they did not ask a thing from us that we were not prepared to give. It is true that we exercised our democratic right of opposing them on the platform and in other ways, when we thought they were wrong. But they were the governing body, and when they said that something should be done, we loyally supported them. That goes for the people from Halifax to Vancouver. To people who have been as loyal as that, and who have the nature to continue to be as loyal as that, no matter who governs this country, it seems to me that the government should give consideration with regard to their needs and desires.
Outside of the places where this increase in freight rates will not be effective because of other factors which enter into the matter, a great many Canadian people will suffer seriously in the operation of their businesses, in the maintenance of their homes, and in all the ways whereby the extra freight rate they will have to pay will affect them when they go to buy the goods and services they require in order to carry on. Is there not some little place in the mind of the government where a little sympathy can edge its way in, gradually expand and grow to a nice big, green tree; not a weeping willow but a tree that will provide shade and comfort for the people of Canada along those lines.
As I say, one can produce piles of evidence to support the statement I made that this is inimical to the people of Canada. But I can use only the argument I have just used in order to try to convince the government that they should at this time reconsider this matter and take action to prevent these proposed increases from coming into effect at this time. If they will do that, they will earn the gratitude of many people in this country. If they do not, they will earn something else; and they will certainly get it.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: The debate, Mr. Speaker, has taken a serious turn this evening.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
I wish to bring to the attention of hon. members the points I want to make. In the first place, I should like to have had more time to put on record some additional arguments for the necessity of a serious consideration of the judgment handed down by the board of transport commissioners. I know among this group there are members who would like strongly to urge the government to reconsider its refusal

Freight Rates
to delay the imposition of the new schedules until the seven provincial premiers have had an opportunity to make their recommendations to the government. When the judgment was handed down by the transport board the Premier of Saskatchewan, Hon. T. C. Douglas, made a public statement in which he said the seven premiers would be lodging a petition to the federal government under section 52(1) of the Railway Act, and I say the action we have witnessed is anti-democratic and certainly shows a cynical disregard for the wishes of the provincial premiers. This is a definite slap in the face to these gentlemen who want to come here and lay their case before the government.
Hon. members from this side who have spoken, and many from the other side, have put on record figures showing clearly that the Canadian Pacific has a surplus this year, and that only the possibility of poor business in future years can justify the additional revenue the increase will give them. Neither I nor any other member of this group would protest increased freight rates as such. We say if it can be shown that the railways need the increases then we are ready to agree to them, but we do not want them imposed in addition to the inequalities which already exist under the freight rate tariff. It has been stated that if the railways were not given these new rates and the larger profits it would mean a general strike of railway employees across this country. That is completely ridiculous. I want to read a statement made by the railways to the board of conciliation in the current wage dispute:
Any relief provided by way of increased rates will not be available for increase of extra costs for the future-such as increased wages-only those up to October, 1945, will be covered.
That should settle that argument.
Getting back to the point I was trying to make, I feel that men who have been elected to parliament do not represent only their particular constituencies but are representatives of the people of Canada, trying to carry out the wishes of those people in order that we may have better relationships, so that our dominion may grow in stature and we may improve the conditions of our people. Last Monday the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) told the members of the Tory party that if the debate could not be concluded by six o'clock the government would adjourn it and take up another matter so that the vote would not be taken that evening. If the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) had co-operated in the same way with this group there would not have been the necessity of carrying on
this debate. However I feel that we have served the people, and my hon. friends opposite who are making so much noise can answer to the people. I believe we have a democratic right to carry on this debate in an effort to see that the decision of the transport board is not allowed to remain in effect. The Premier of Saskatchewan said if these rates were allowed to go into operation they would bring chaos, and that if the decision were reversed later, after representations had been made, a great deal of confusion would result. That is what has happened; and, as I said before, I think the action taken by the government was a slap in the face to the seven provincial premiers who are coming here on April 24 to meet the cabinet. In the past these same premiers have co-operated with the government at interprovincial conferences, and I think they should have been shown a little courtesy.

subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Since I had an opportunity to discuss this matter in the house a few days ago, I have received from my constituency telegrams and resolutions which indicate that the people of western Canada will not accept the increase in freight rates without protest.
I find that the judgment of the board of transport commissioners sets out that the rates in the standard and special freight tariffs may be increased by 21 per cent. We find the word "may" appearing throughout the judgment, apparently leaving it to the railway companies to decide whether the increase shall be put into effect in some parts of the country and not in others. I have been told of the increase the poultry producers in Saskatchewan have been compelled to pay. Previously I understand that they enjoyed a rate of thirty-five cents for a thirty-dozen crate of eggs, and that this rate has now been increased to seventy-five cents.
I move the adjournment of the debate, Mr. Speaker.
On motion of Mr. Nicholson the debate was adjourned.
What will be the business tomorrow?

Tomorrow we hope to deal with the motion of the Minister of Agriculture for second reading of Bill No. 204, to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Then we should like to go into committee of the whole on the Unemployment Insurance Act. Then we shall take up the Dominion
Business of the House

Elections Act, and any other items on the order paper not yet disposed of. We had hoped to be able to go into supply in the Department of Agriculture, and in the Department of External Affairs on Monday next, but unfortunately that has not been possible.
Will the minister give any indication as to when the freight rates debate will go on?
Not at this time.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
